Molecular dynamics still supplies the local chemistry, but the pore geometry becomes a design variable for a given application.

title: Dynamically Reentrant Skyrmion Phase in Oscillating Magnetic Fields
abstract: We address a central open question in driven topological matter by investigating the nonequilibrium response of a two-dimensional magnet with Dzyaloshinskii-Moriya interactions subjected to a periodically oscillating magnetic field. Using extensive Monte Carlo simulations, we uncover a dynamically reentrant skyrmion phase that emerges within a finite window of field amplitudes and bias fields, sandwiched between the conventional skyrmion and polarized ferromagnetic phases. This phase has no equilibrium counterpart and originates from an imbalance between skyrmion creation and annihilation over a single field cycle, leading to a reversal of the period-averaged topological charge. We show that the re-entrant phase exists only in the dynamic response regime where the system can follow the drive, and is suppressed at higher driving frequencies. Our results establish periodic driving as a nonequilibrium control parameter for stabilizing and reversing skyrmion topology.

title: Directional Control of Chiral Polymer Emission Dissymmetry by Plasmonic Metasurfaces
abstract: Circularly polarized (CP) emission is central to next-generation photonic and optoelectronic technologies, yet simultaneously controlling its directionality, intensity, and handedness remains a major challenge. Advances in molecular and materials design have enabled strong chiral light-matter interactions and large dissymmetry between opposite CP states. However, conventional thin-film architectures provide limited control over the angular distribution of CP emission and often exhibit strongly angle-dependent chiral emission. Metasurfaces, on the other hand, offer powerful control over emission directionality and polarization, but have predominantly been explored with intrinsically achiral emitters. For the first time, we integrate organic chiral polymer thin films with planar chiral plasmonic metasurfaces to enhance chiral light-matter interactions while controlling the directionality and angular dependence of chiral emission. Using angle-resolved Stokes Fourier polarimetry, we show that metasurface coupling produces directional emission, near-normal dissymmetry factors exceeding 0.7, and, remarkably, direction-dependent reversal of the emission handedness at fixed molecular stereochemistry.

title: A Design Rule for Passive Reconfigurable Microwave Devices
abstract: Every reconfigurable microwave device places a tuning element - a varactor, a diode, transistor, microelectromechanical or phase-change switch, a ferroelectric or liquid-crystal load - inside a fixed passive network. The network can make a small change of the element produce a large change of the response, and design practice often credits it with the device's tuning capability. This paper shows that a fixed, linear, passive network cannot add to that capability. Each tuning element carries a tuning budget, a dimensionless length computed from its own impedance trajectory, and a fixed passive network can transmit that budget or lose part of it, never enlarge it. The unit of the budget is the hyperbolic distance of the Smith chart: the distance from a match is the logarithm of the voltage standing-wave ratio, and the distance between two states sets their mutual mismatch and is the logarithm of their commutation quality factor. From one inequality we derive closed-form, ready-to-use limits for analog and digital phase shifters, true-time-delay lines, switches, attenuators, vector modulators, impedance tuners, tunable filters, reconfigurable antennas, metasurface cells and multiport networks; the two-state and attenuation limits are attained by explicit circuits, and the phase limit by a constant-loss trajectory. We introduce the $Λ$-chart, a Smith-chart companion on which budgets and requirements are read graphically, and apply it to four published microwave case studies.

title: Local information processing capacity: anatomy of computation in neuromorphic systems
abstract: Many neuromorphic systems possess rich internal computational structures shaped by their physical dynamics. However, existing metrics characterize only global computation, leaving these local structures unresolved despite their importance for system interpretation, optimization and miniaturization. Here, we introduce local information processing capacity (L-IPC), which represents individual dynamical states as vectors in an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space and decomposes their computational properties through subspace projections onto nonlinearity orders and memory steps, with the residual quantifying computational irrelevance. Applied to three systems with comparable global capacities (an echo state network, an ion-gating reservoir and a spin-wave reservoir), L-IPC reveals markedly different distributions of computation, ranging from homogeneous to spatially, temporally and spectrally structured patterns. These local profiles further guide task-specific pruning, outperforming standard approaches at the same size in the structured systems. These results establish L-IPC as a general framework for anatomizing computation and guiding task-adaptive design in neuromorphic systems.

title: Low cross-plane thermal conductivity of $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films
abstract: The thermal conductivities of (001) $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ thin films deposited on $c$-plane sapphire substrates were measured with frequency-domain thermoreflectance (FDTR). The thermal conductivity increases from 1.83 $^{+0.19}_{-0.18}$ W/m$\cdot$K to 2.26 $^{+0.35}_{-0.40}$ W/m$\cdot$K as the thicknesses increase from 159 nm to 689 nm. This weak thickness dependence indicates that the majority of the intrinsic phonon mean free paths are smaller than the range of investigated film thicknesses. First-principles-based calculations that include phonon-phonon and phonon-boundary scattering capture this size-dependent behavior and support our experimental observation. Temperature-dependent measurements of a 689 nm film from 293 to 400 K show a decrease in thermal conductivity with increasing temperature due to enhanced phonon-phonon scattering. A weaker temperature dependence is observed in a 159 nm film where phonon-boundary scattering becomes more prominent. At comparable film thicknesses, our measured $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ films exhibit lower values of cross-plane thermal conductivity than the other experimentally measured Ga$_2$O$_3$ polymorphs. Our experimental observations are supported by prior predictions, which suggest that the low thermal conductivity of $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$ results from its complex crystal structure, which leads to increased anharmonicity and lower phonon group velocities relative to other polymorphs. Thermal management strategies, such as integration with high-thermal-conductivity substrates, may thus be required to mitigate self-heating for $κ$-Ga$_2$O$_3$-based electronic devices.

title: Analog signal processing, storage, and demultiplexing via in-materia wave-based computing
abstract: The ability of mechanical systems to perform basic computations has gained traction in recent years, providing a robust supplement to digital computing in off-grid, low-power, and extreme environments where electronics are inaccessible or risk failure. However, prior work has focused on Boolean logic applied via bistable structures, snap-through mechanisms, or origami lattices. Digital signal processing (DSP) underpins a wide range of computational tasks, providing the foundation for information encoding, manipulation, and analysis. In contrast to conventional DSP approaches, we present a new paradigm for analog information processing, where an elastic substrate houses a spatial wave-based platform for mechanical signal manipulation in the temporal domain. The proposed metasurface-based system exploits temperature-dependent phase transitions of shape memory alloys (SMAs) to realize key signal-processing functionalities, including gating, retention, and programmable delay of impinging mechanical loads. In doing so, we address a new set of challenges by manipulating transient mechanical waves through dispersive and lossy media. Building on this capability, we introduce the concept of mechanical wave-based memory, in which a locally resonant metamaterial's dispersion characteristics are actively reconfigured to achieve programmable delays while preserving spatial waveform integrity, and demonstrate its utility in the context of input shaping and frequency demultiplexing of superimposed waves. More broadly, the modular and scalable nature of the demonstrated framework paves the way for advanced mechanical computing architectures, enabling higher-order operations such as signal classification, parallel processing, and reservoir computing through the controlled sequencing and temporal alignment of mechanical signals.

title: Periodically poled lithium niobate with submicrometer periodicity using electric-field poling technique
abstract: A series of monocrystalline lithium niobate (LN) thin films on low-resistivity silicon (LNOS) substrates, with thicknesses ranging from micrometers down to tens of nanometers, were prepared through chemical-mechanical polishing of pristine crystal films. By employing the electric-field poling technique, high-quality periodically poled lithium niobate (PPLN) structures with submicrometer periodicity were fabricated in these LNOSs, and full-thickness polarization reversal beneath the poling electrodes with a well-defined depth profile was achieved. The coercive field was found to follow the Kay-Dunn scaling law, while the lateral domain broadening generally increased with increasing film thickness, and it remained approximately constant across different electrode linewidths at a given film thickness. PPLN structures with periods ranging from 6 $μ$m down to 200 nm were demonstrated. These findings provide guidance for poling electrode design and lateral domain broadening pre-compensation, offering a practical route toward scalable domain engineering in LN thin films with promising potential for compact and highly integrated nonlinear photonic devices.

title: Low-Terahertz Channel Performance in Falling Wheat for Moisture Sensing
abstract: Terahertz (THz) waves are highly sensitive to water and therefore offer a promising noncontact approach to wheat moisture sensing, but existing THz studies have been limited to static samples. This article investigates moisture sensing based on the performance of a THz channel in falling wheat, as encountered at grain intake. The channel power loss is measured at six frequencies from 120 to 320 GHz for three moisture contents and interpreted with a physics-based model that couples the double-Debye permittivity of water, Landau-Lifshitz-Looyenga mixing, and Lorenz-Mie extinction. The model reproduces the measured loss. Above the extinction maximum, the dielectric moisture response peaks where the wavelength approaches the kernel diameter, and that a two-frequency loss ratio removes the loading dependence. A channel-level analysis of QPSK and 16-QAM links shows that a 1 dB moisture-induced loss change alters the bit error rate (BER) by a factor of 3 to 30. THz communication channels at grain intake could therefore sense moisture as a byproduct of data transmission.

title: Emergence of Berry curvature dipole and nonlinear Hall effect in a novel hexagonal borophosphene allotrope
abstract: We investigate the electronic structure, local orbital coupling, and strain-tunable nonlinear Hall response of two arsenic-substituted borophosphene-derived monolayers, As@MBP and As@AMBP, using first-principles calculations and tight-binding analysis. In the absence of spin--orbit coupling, both systems exhibit a finite Berry-curvature dipole (BCD) and a substantial nonlinear Hall conductivity, demonstrating that the nonlinear response is intrinsically driven by orbital physics and inversion-symmetry breaking. $As$ substitution opens sizable band gaps of $120~\mathrm{meV}$ in As@MBP and $90~\mathrm{meV}$ in As@AMBP, well exceeding room-temperature thermal fluctuations ($k_{\mathrm{B}}T \approx 25.9~\mathrm{meV}$). Tight-binding analysis reveals that $As$ incorporation breaks the equivalence of $B-P$ hoppings in As@MBP and induces sign reversals in key nearest-neighbor hoppings in As@AMBP, reflecting a pronounced electronic reconstruction beyond simple geometric effects. Under mechanical strain, the redistribution of Berry curvature yields a maximum BCD of $22~\mathring{\text{A}}$ in As@MBP, approximately $10$ times larger than that of unstrained structure, and induces a reversal of the BCD sign. These results establish $As$-substituted borophosphene derivatives as promising light-element platforms for mechanically switchable nonlinear transport and quantum-material applications without relying on strong spin-orbit coupling.

title: Hall-Density Collapse as Direct Evidence for Percolative Conduction Onset in Monolayer MoS$_2$ Transistors
authors: C. J. L. de la Rosa
abstract: The origin of the apparent metal-insulator transition in two-dimensional electron systems remains debated. Using temperature-dependent transport and Hall measurements on industry-relevant MoS$_2$ monolayer FETs with amorphous HfO$_2$ dielectrics, we establish classical percolation as the underlying mechanism. We report two complementary signatures of disorder-driven conduction onset: a temperature-independent Hall-density collapse as a function of absolute gate voltage and a vanishing activation energy at a characteristic carrier density $n_{\mathrm{c}}$, identified as the percolation threshold. These findings identify dielectric-interface disorder, rather than channel quality alone, as the key parameter governing device turn-on. The extracted activation barriers reach values substantially exceeding room-temperature thermal energies, indicating that disorder-driven conduction onset remains relevant well beyond cryogenic transport.

title: Photonic and Electronic Interaction of TMD-Hybridized ZnO Nanowire Lasers
abstract: Semiconductor nanowire lasers are promising on-chip coherent light sources for photonic integrated circuits, but integration inevitably places them in contact with other materials, thereby changing their properties upon hybridization. In this study, we examine the photonic and electronic coupling between single ZnO nanowire lasers and TMDs. Using deterministic nanomanipulation, we first hybridized the same nanowire first with a WS$_2$ monolayer and then with a MoS$_2$ monolayer. The respective lasing threshold rises, the emission is strongly quenched at high pump power densities, and the mode envelope blueshifts. Upon hybridization with bilayer, trilayer, and bulk MoS$_2$, lasing is fully suppressed. Finite-Difference Eigenmode simulations show that the TMD absorbs part of the evanescent field. Because this absorption is wavelength dependent, it also removes modes from the low-energy flank of the envelope, which accounts for small difference between the two monolayers, while the blueshift itself follows the increase of the carrier density at threshold. Density functional theory calculations that include the interface dipole predict a type-I alignment at the ideal ZnO(10$\bar{1}$0)/TMD interface, which turns into type~II for a moderately reduced dipole, as expected for hydroxylated facets in air. In both cases, holes are transferred from the nanowire into the TMD and removed from the gain medium. Evanescent absorption and hole transfer thus jointly suppress lasing, and both must be accounted for when integrating nanowire lasers with 2D materials.

title: Hyperbolic Nanocavities for Single-Molecule Vibrational Strong Coupling
abstract: Hyperbolic phonon polaritons (HPhPs) in low-loss anisotropic materials such as hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) provide extreme sub-diffractional field confinement in the mid-infrared, making them attractive for enhancing the interaction of light with molecular vibrations. Collective vibrational strong coupling between molecular ensembles and HPhPs has already been demonstrated in extended slabs. Reaching this regime with a single molecule, however, remains a major challenge, and would provide a platform for investigating how vacuum electromagnetic fields influence molecular dynamics and chemical reactivity. Here, we show theoretically that single-molecule vibrational strong coupling can be reached in hBN nanocavities that laterally confine HPhPs within a finite volume. Combining full-wave electromagnetic simulations with the few-mode quantization approach, we find that these nanocavities support a rich set of asymmetric resonances that strongly enhance the local spectral density, with frequencies that follow from simple HPhP ray trajectories and can be tuned through the cavity aspect ratio. We identify resonances with quality factors of about $600$ and effective mode volumes of $|V_{\mathrm{eff}}| \sim 10^{-7}λ^{3}$, sufficient for single-molecule strong coupling with vibrational transitions with dipole moments on the order of $1\,\mathrm{D}$. These results establish hyperbolic nanocavities as a promising platform for single-molecule vibrational strong coupling and open new routes toward the local control of vibrational dynamics and molecular energy flow.

title: Spin swapping mediated by spin-orbital textures in centrosymmetric multiorbital materials
abstract: Spin swapping converts a primary spin current into a secondary one by interchanging its flow and spin-polarization directions, attributed to spin-orbit scattering or spin-band splitting. Here we uncover a fundamentally distinct route to spin swapping arising from the orbital degree of freedom in the spin pumping to centrosymmetric multiorbital materials \textit{without spin-band splitting}. When the dynamical proximity ferromagnet injects a longitudinal spin current flowing normal to the interface, spin-orbit-entangled orbital textures redirect the injected spins into longitudinal and transverse orbital currents. Their subsequent conversion back to the spin sector generates transverse spin currents with propagation and polarization directions swapped relative to the primary spin current. The swapping efficiency achieves $50\%$ for Ge and Si. Governed by a fourth-rank tensor constrained by crystalline symmetry and without requiring spin-orbit scattering or inversion symmetry breaking, our finding reveals spin-orbital textures as hidden intermediate channels of spin swapping with unexplored material choices and functionalities.

title: Electrostatics of Chern junctions in a magnetic field
abstract: Electrostatic control is central to the operation of semiconductor junctions made from conventional materials. Here, we theoretically investigate the electrostatic properties of lateral junctions between two-dimensional (2D) Chern semiconductors in a perpendicular magnetic field. The spectral asymmetry of a Chern semiconductor acts as a magnetic-field-induced effective dopant density that is dependent on the Chern number. As a consequence, two regions with different Chern numbers acquire different chemical potentials at charge neutrality, leading to a built-in potential of topological origin across the junction. Using this built-in potential as a boundary condition, we solve the 2D Poisson equation to obtain the electric potential and charge density profiles, as well as the capacitance, of Chern semiconductor junctions. Our results inform the interplay between electronic topology and electrostatics in devices made from 2D materials.

title: Spin Simulators based on Exciton-Polariton Waveguide Networks
abstract: Many NP-hard optimization problems can be mapped onto interacting spin systems, whose ground state encodes the optimal solution. Polaritonic implementations based on gain-dissipative dynamics have recently emerged as promising analog computing platforms owing to their intrinsic parallelism and ultrafast operation. However, existing approaches are hindered by two fundamental limitations: maintaining the homogeneous amplitudes required for faithful problem encoding remains challenging in realistic physical systems, and most architectures are restricted to nearest-neighbour interactions, severely limiting the variety of optimization problems that can be efficiently addressed. We introduce a feasible polaritonic XY simulator based on a reconfigurable waveguide platform that overcomes both limitations. Our approach guarantees amplitude homogeneity while enabling the implementa- tion of arbitrary symmetric coupling matrices, thereby allowing the direct encoding of a wide variety of XY Hamiltonians. These results establish a practical architecture for programmable polaritonic spin simulators and pave the way towards scalable optical hardware for analog optimisation.

title: The quantized Hall effect knows which way the current flows: mirror covariance and rectification in a laterally asymmetric Hall bar
abstract: The quantized Hall effect is the textbook emblem of universality: a resistance fixed by $h/e^2$, apparently indifferent to the shape of the sample, to its edges and to the direction of the current. That indifference is only half true. The plateau value is universal; the plateau is not. In a gate-defined Hall bar with one hard and one soft edge, reversing the current moves the plateau edge, and exchanging the edges reverses the move. We identify the symmetry that forces this. Because a perpendicular field breaks time reversal, the relevant operation is the in-plane $C_2$ rotation; within the self-consistent screening model it gives the covariance relation $R_α[B,V_{\mathrm{conf}}(x),I]=R_α[B,V_{\mathrm{conf}}(-x),-I]$, exact deep in the nonlinear regime and independent of linear response or microscopic reversibility. It predicts a rectification that is odd under exchange of the gate voltages and reverses with the magnetic field. The field-reversal test leaves the frozen lateral disorder untouched, so it holds for a single sample; it has not yet been performed. A further measurement, collapsing one incompressible strip, discriminates between co-directed and chiral pictures of the current. Self-consistent calculations show the soft-edge strip widening from 69 to 106\,nm on current reversal, moving the Hall resistance from 0.940 to $0.999994\,h/2e^2$ within a bounded window in magnetic field. The effect is a gate-tunable vector-product nonreciprocity, not magnetochiral anisotropy.

title: cuRoboV2-Fast: Fast Torque-Limited Collision-Free Motion Planning
abstract: We present cuRoboV2-Fast, a GPU-accelerated planner that reduces both planning latency and execution time for collision-free, payload-aware, torque-limited motions. B-spline trajectory optimization reduces the required iterations, while accelerated robot computations and differentiable inverse dynamics reduce refinement cost and accommodate changing payloads. TimeOpt optimizes traversal speed along the fixed path under sampled velocity, acceleration, jerk, and torque constraints, exploiting local spline support to solve banded Newton systems efficiently on the GPU. With a 3,kg payload, cuRoboV2-Fast achieves 4.4 ms mean planning time on RTX 5090, 14.7x faster than cuRoboV2. Our method on Jetson AGX Orin plans faster than cuRoboV1 + TOPPRA on RTX 5090. A stereo-camera-based deployment on YAM achieves 5.93 s mean completed pick-and-drop cycles, 34.6% shorter than cuRoboV2. Code (Apache 2.0): www.github.com/NVlabs/curobo , Project Page: www.research.nvidia.com/labs/lpr/curobov2-fast .

title: VABAR: A Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics
abstract: For robots to operate reliably in commercial and industrial applications, they must persistently perform specific tasks with known variations in object shape and pose. We call this Variational Automation (VA) to differentiate these settings from fixed automation. Inspired by recent papers on Agentic Robotics, where pretrained LLM and VLM coding agents combine interpretable robot programming with the open-world adaptability of model free policies, we propose a general set of agentic robotics benchmark design criteria that includes accessibility, repeatability, diversity, relevance to agentic robotics and practical applications, physical realizability, resistance to benchmark saturation, and computational efficiency. We instantiate these principles in six manipulation task classes spanning industrial, medical, and infrastructure applications: tool sorting, tool hanging, gear meshing, syringe packing, cable insertion, and cable routing. We introduce the Variational Automation Benchmark for Agentic Robotics (VABAR), an open, easily replicable, simulation-based manipulation benchmark to systematically evaluating agentic robotics systems. Built fully on open-source tools, VABAR features detailed implementations using the Newton physics engine, standardized task variations, difficulty tiers, success metrics, and a library of 33 generalizable skills with human-authored programmatic reference solutions. We provide initial baseline evaluations using an open agentic manipulation harness, Graph-as-Policy (GaP), and Isaac Lab Arena.

title: Rethinking Self-Repair in Code-as-Policy Agents: What Drives Retry Success?
abstract: Code-as-policy agents often use execution feedback to retry failed programs. Additional sampling and task guidance can also improve success, leaving the contribution of failure-specific feedback unclear. We study this question in simulated robot manipulation. A fixed lookup selects feedback templates using failure labels and the API variant. A frozen code model generates a fresh program after each scene reset. On the same 252 initial failures, Qwen2.5-Coder-7B recovers 85.3% within five retries, compared with 68.3% for resampling with the same retry cap. The advantage persists under fixed total-token budgets. Feedback from other episodes and fixed task guidance yield similar recovery point estimates, with no detected benefit from matching the coarse failure label. In a separate study, a fixed guided prompt used from the first attempt achieves an observed overall success rate similar to that of template-based feedback. Template-based feedback also lowers recovery on a nut-insertion task requiring a rim grasp, consistent with an incompatible center-grasp instruction. Evaluations of robot self-repair should include resampling, mismatched feedback, and concise, task-compatible static guidance as baselines.

title: Human Mobility Sensing Using Wall-Reflected Beamformed Millimeter-Wave Communication Signals
abstract: Existing millimeter-wave (mmWave) communication beam patterns spatially weight human-scattered signals and shape the received-power signatures induced by human motion. We exploit these beam-shaped signatures for device-free walkingpace and walk-direction classification using a wall-reflected 60.8-GHz link with closely spaced phased arrays and fixed communication beamforming vectors. Human movement alters the interference between wall-reflected and scattered signals, producing power oscillations surrounding a central blockage fade. A beam-dependent interference model provides a physical interpretation of these signatures. Using received-power statistics from a continuous-tone experiment, we extract fade duration for walking-pace classification and pre/post-fade asymmetries for walk-direction classification. Measurements comprise 144 crossings from three participants along perpendicular and diagonal trajectories. Under leave-one-participant-out validation, logistic regression achieves 86.1% binary and 79.2% three-class walking pace accuracy, and 77.1% travel-direction accuracy. The results demonstrate mobility sensing using fixed communication beams without channel estimation, Doppler processing, or dedicated radar hardware

title: Risk-Sensitive Stochastic Optimal Control on Positive Cones
abstract: We consider stochastic optimal control problems in which the state is constrained to a proper cone. Specifically, we consider risk-neutral, risk-averse, and risk-seeking formulations within a single entropic-risk framework. We investigate classes of problems whose Bellman operator preserves affine functions and characterize their optimal value functions and feedback policies for both finite-horizon and time-average infinite-horizon problems. Additionally, we establish convergence and state-bound results under finite-step cost observability. Moreover, we demonstrate an exact connection between entropic-risk optimal control on proper cones and deterministic infsup control for systems whose dynamics and stage costs are affine in the disturbances. In addition, we provide examples of classes of systems for which explicit solutions can be obtained.

title: Extremal-Phase-Guided Sequential Convex Optimization: Model Order Reduction
abstract: Fixed-order frequency-weighted H-infinity approximation is a nonconvex problem, and local optimization methods can be sensitive to initialization. We present extremal-phase-guided sequential convex optimization (EPGSCO) for stable fixed-order rational approximation. We introduce a novel phase-guidance technique motivated by the all-pass structure underlying optimal Hankel-norm approximation, with a phase template fitted to the error-magnitude derivative at dominant peaks. We integrate this guidance with dominant-peak selection, focused frequency grids, and adaptive pole-residue and polynomial-coefficient updates to address stagnation and improve approximation accuracy. CD-player examples and benchmarks with known optimal errors evaluate the algorithm against established methods. Comparisons with classical sequential convex optimization (SCO) under shared settings for the common components assess the combined contribution of phase guidance and adaptive frequency refinement. Results demonstrate improved accuracy in most of the tested cases and attainment of the known optimum from four tested initializations for a constructed order-42 benchmark, with additional computation in some cases.

title: Excitability of High-Frequency Positive Feedback
abstract: What is the threshold of an excitable system, i.e. the criterion that distinguishes rest from excitation? Previous research has shown that this question is far from trivial to answer. This paper studies the threshold of a simple excitable primitive in which excitability arises from the positive feedback interconnection of a first-order high-pass filter and a static, strictly monotone and strictly convex activation function. This threshold is a simple inequality on the difference between the instantaneous input and the motif's internal memory. While this result may help neuro-engineers characterize spiking in biological and artificial neurons, we argue that excitability is not always a desirable property, and that our threshold may also be relevant to safety considerations in fragile systems with rate-induced tipping points. We illustrate our framework with three examples: the FitzHugh-Nagumo model of neuronal dynamics, a model of stop-loss cascades in the stock market, and a social contagion model.

title: CMS ECAL Phase-2 upgrade: characterisation and stability analysis of a three-stage low-voltage power-conversion system
abstract: As part of the High-Luminosity upgrade of the Large Hadron Collider, the front-end electronics of the Compact Muon Solenoid electromagnetic calorimeter barrel are being replaced. A three-stage low-voltage power-conversion system supplies the upgraded electronics. As the cascade dynamics require characterisation to ensure stable operation, interactions between the three converter stages are assessed at their two interfaces using the Nyquist criterion. A validated shunt-injection setup using a Bode 100 frequency-response analyser provides in-situ impedance measurements under load to assess the accuracy of the averaged converter models. Results show that both interfaces are stable over the evaluated configurations, with modelled minimum distances to the critical point of 0.76 and 0.79, respectively. A turn-on study identifies capacitor charging at Stage 3 as the main cause of inrush currents triggering Stage 2 overcurrent protection. Two Stage 3 board variants stagger converter enables within and between boards, keeping the measured two-tower current below 5 A, within the 8.0 A protection threshold.

title: Optimal Holding Times for Entanglement Swapping
abstract: We revisit the optimization of entanglement holding times in memory-based quantum repeaters for maximizing entanglement swapping throughput under different fidelity constraints - strict, probabilistic, and mean. We consider two heterogeneous quantum links that are equipped with single or multiple memories and differ in decoherence rates, memory capacities, entanglement attempt rates and success probabilities, as well as classical communication latencies. Efficient models are developed to estimate the expected entanglement throughput and the probability density functions of the conditional wait time to swap. The models are then used to satisfy different fidelity requirements by optimizing the maximum holding times for the two links. Finally, our proposed model and approach are validated with a discrete-event quantum network simulator.

title: Deterministic Oracle Complexity for Goldstein Stationarity in Nonsmooth Nonconvex Optimization with Constraints
abstract: We consider the deterministic oracle complexity of finding a $(δ,ε)$-Goldstein stationary point of a Lipschitz function under constraints. The problem is posed in $\mathbb{R}^d$, where $d$ denotes the dimension; constraints are specified either by a closed feasible set or by a single explicit inequality. For closed feasible sets that are star-shaped with respect to an interior ball, including all convex bodies, we use a resisting-oracle construction to show that every deterministic algorithm needs $Ω(ε^{-2})$ objective-oracle calls in the worst case when $d\gtrsimε^{-2}$ and $δ\lesssimε$. For explicit inequalities satisfying uniform Goldstein constraint qualification and strict feasibility, finding Goldstein KKT stationary points requires exponentially many oracle calls in $d$ in the worst case, even at fixed stationarity accuracy. This exponential dependence holds under dimension-independent constraint regularity and strict-feasibility bounds, with a sufficiently small neighborhood radius and complementary slackness error. The result covers common constraints such as ball and box constraints and also allows nonconvex feasible regions. For convex coercive constraints with a Slater point, the resisting-oracle argument also gives an $Ω(ε^{-2})$ oracle-call bound in the same dimension and radius regime while allowing a larger complementary slackness error. These results hold for all deterministic algorithms using a local oracle, whether or not the returned point was queried. Each constructed objective has a strictly feasible global minimizer; the lower bounds therefore concern the information required to find stationary points, not their existence.

title: Odd Capillarity
abstract: Capillarity governs interfacial relaxation and hydrodynamic motion in binary fluids through parity-even mechanical stresses. Here, we introduce \emph{odd capillarity}, a parity-breaking interfacial mechanical response, by incorporating a symmetric, nonvariational, parity-odd capillary stress into the Cahn--Hilliard--Navier--Stokes (CHNS) equations. This stress generates forces along interfaces, transverse to ordinary capillary forces, and performs mechanical work that is not balanced by changes in the composition free energy. Direct numerical simulations reveal that odd capillarity arrests domain coarsening while sustaining turbulent fluid motion without a conventional inertial energy cascade, as energy injection is predominantly balanced by viscous dissipation. In asymmetric mixtures, odd capillarity driven deformation and breakup interrupt droplet growth, producing dynamically arrested emulsions with composition hyperuniformity and suppressed large-scale vorticity fluctuations. These findings establish odd capillarity as a distinct interfacial mechanism for controlling phase separation and sustaining nonequilibrium fluid motion.

title: Experimental evaluation of Kolmogorov's first similarity hypothesis for shear-dependent viscosity fluids
abstract: We experimentally investigate the applicability of Kolmogorov's first similarity hypothesis to shear-dependent viscosity fluids. We assess whether dissipative range statistics exhibit a self-similar behavior in nearly homogeneous and isotropic turbulence, using stereo particle image velocimetry in aqueous Carbopol solutions across two concentrations and a range of forcing conditions. We observe that, when normalized by the mean viscosity and mean dissipation rate, second- and third-order structure functions collapse across the different experimental conditions and exhibit functional forms compatible with classical Newtonian results. These observations are in general agreement with the recent numerical results of Rosti [J. Fluid Mech. 1012, R5 (2025)], who proposed that Kolmogorov's similarity hypotheses can be extended to shear-thinning fluids by considering dissipation scales based on the mean viscosity, the mean dissipation rate, and the flow index.

title: Interscale energy transfer in a propeller-driven homogeneous and isotropic turbulence generation device
abstract: We investigate the interscale energy dynamics of nearly homogeneous isotropic turbulence (HIT) generated in a spherically forced, propeller-driven device. From a spatial perspective, by employing the Kármán-Howarth-Monin (KHM) framework, we analyze the scale-by-scale energy transfer without isotropy assumptions. In contrast to other forcing strategies, where regions with inverse and forward cascades often coexist in scale space, we show that spherical forcing produces a purely forward energy cascade across the entire scale space. While the energy distribution remains highly isotropic and orientation-averaged structure functions align with Kolmogorov's two-thirds law, the energy flux exhibits a directional dependence, suggesting a higher sensitivity to residual forcing asymmetries. Regarding the temporal dynamics, the reduced mean flow generated by this device allows us to investigate the temporal variability in conditions where Taylor's frozen turbulence hypothesis does not apply. Our results provide experimental validation of Tennekes' Eulerian frequency spectrum, where intermediate scales evidence an inertial-convective range with statistics determined by the integral velocity scale and the dissipation rate. Finally, we adopt a global approach to investigate whether the main turbulent scales can be linked to external experimental parameters. We propose a framework that captures the propeller frequency dependence of the main turbulent variables obtained in our measurements and those of previously reported HIT chambers. These findings contribute to the understanding of how external forcing influences the complex interscale energy dynamics of turbulent flows from a spatial, temporal, and global perspective.

title: A Drift-Diffusion Approach for Pearson Type IV Heavy-Tail Distributions
abstract: Non-Gaussian stationary fluctuations with heavy tails and finite-order moment cutoffs are ubiquitous in non-equilibrium systems. Here, we derive the Pearson type IV distribution as the stationary solution of a standardized Fokker-Planck equation with linear drift and quadratic diffusion. We establish necessary and sufficient conditions for its emergence and show that the linear-quadratic structure, although sufficient, is not necessary. We also give explicit closed expressions for the cumulative distribution function, a moment recurrence relation, skewness, kurtosis, and mode. From a physical perspective, our results reveal that heavy tails and asymmetry originate from distinct features of state-dependent diffusion: its local nonlinear curvature and gradient, respectively. In particular, asymmetric stationary fluctuations can emerge even in the presence of a symmetric linear restoring drift. This framework provides a general stochastic description of asymmetric heavy-tailed fluctuations in non-equilibrium systems, including space plasma turbulence.

title: To lift or not to lift: Operator inference for nonlinear PDEs with boundary control
abstract: Operator inference (OpInf) provides a nonintrusive framework for learning projection-based reduced-order models directly from data, but its standard formulations do not explicitly account for the fact that boundary actuation changes the admissible solution space of a PDE. This paper develops and evaluates a boundary-consistent, lifting-based OpInf formulation for nonlinear PDEs with time-varying inhomogeneous boundary conditions. The proposed approach decomposes the state into a known lifting component that satisfies the prescribed boundary conditions and a homogeneous component represented in a POD basis. Substituting this decomposition into the governing dynamics reveals a boundary-consistent reduced model structure in which the learned dynamics includes bilinear state-input and quadratic input-input interactions for quadratically nonlinear PDEs. The resulting operators are inferred from data, preserving the nonintrusive character of OpInf while guaranteeing boundary condition satisfaction by construction. Numerical experiments on boundary-actuated heat, Burgers, and lid-driven cavity problems show that the lifted formulation improves boundary compliance and can enhance prediction accuracy, solver stability, and computational efficiency, although these gains vary across problems and reduced model dimensions. Overall, this study establishes lifting as a principled extension of OpInf for boundary-actuated PDEs, clarifies when and how this formulation improves performance, and indicates that standard OpInf can remain an effective alternative in certain regimes.

title: Amortized Optimization for Calibrating Stochastic Social Simulators
abstract: Stochastic simulators need suitable parameter values to reproduce observed behaviour in complex systems. Searching for these values through repeated simulations makes frequent recalibration computationally expensive. We develop an amortized optimizer that uses simulations collected in advance to learn how to choose parameters that make simulated outcomes agree with observations. Once fitted, it maps new observations to feasible parameters without further simulator calls. The method retains alternative parameter settings that can explain similar observations and compares their responses, avoiding the conflicting labels that arise when training a single parameter regressor. Historical observations also provide supervision by showing which simulated responses agree with the data, even when the underlying parameters are unknown. Experiments across four simulators compare calibration accuracy and query time. Dedicated cost analyses quantify traffic preparation and the recorded financial reuse costs.On new traffic targets, local correction more than halves query time relative to empirical and surrogate selection; a learned inverse is faster still, with similar mean error. In a retrospective comparison on real financial data, our method returns parameters about $1.07\times10^{7}$ times faster than a 10-minute Gaussian-process Bayesian optimization search, with mean calibration error 3.06% higher. Reusing simulation work across observations supports repeated parameter updates when the available time is too short for a new search.

title: InterSim: Innovative Intersection Digital Twins for Human-in-the-Loop Driving Simulation
abstract: Innovative intersection designs can improve roadway safety and operational efficiency, but their uncommon geometries may create challenges for driver comprehension during early deployment. Evaluating these designs through full-scale field implementation can also be costly. This paper presents InterSim, a Unity game engine-based human-in-the-loop (HITL) driving simulator that constructs digital twins of site-specific innovative intersections in a virtual environment. InterSim links the real world and the simulation world through two closed cycles: a digital twin cycle that builds each intersection twin from agency design and traffic data and returns evidence from simulation to the agency, and an HITL cycle in which human drivers or automated driving algorithms operate the ego vehicle under identical scenario conditions. The research capabilities of InterSim are demonstrated through two case studies: a surrogate safety study compares post-encroachment time distributions between a Reduced Conflict Intersection and a standard intersection under different traffic volumes; an eco-driving study compares human drivers with a rule-based agent using vehicle-to-infrastructure information and reveals differences in emission and driving behavior. These studies demonstrate that InterSim provides a reusable digital twin platform for investigating innovative intersection designs from diverse perspectives. Demo video and open-source code can be accessed at https://purduedigitaltwin.github.io/InterSim/

title: One Basket, Many Experts: Decorrelated Re-ranking for Financial Asset Recommendation
abstract: Financial asset recommendation for retail investors is typically optimized for relevance, that is, how well a recommendation matches what each user will buy. From the service provider's point of view, the value of a recommendation also depends on portfolio performance: the risk-adjusted return the recommended assets (the basket) deliver, which drives user engagement and fee revenue. The two goals are rarely achieved jointly, because the recommendations that best match user behavior concentrate on a few popular assets whose returns are highly correlated, which caps the risk-adjusted return a provider can offer. We propose Decorrelated-Satellite Expert Re-ranking (\textbf{DSER}), which retains the most relevant recommendations from an expert-following list and replaces the rest with return-decorrelated alternatives. The number of replaced slots is a single integer~$m$ (a knob) that the provider sets, so the relevance--performance trade-off becomes an explicit, auditable choice rather than a property hidden inside a learned model. In experiments on the public FAR-Trans retail-brokerage dataset, under the primary protocol, replacing a few slots improves risk-adjusted return at a small relevance cost, and the gain survives realistic trading costs at typical retail portfolio sizes. Minimizing correlation would lower basket volatility, but in our data the least-correlated assets are more volatile and higher-return, so their volatility offsets that reduction while their return drives the gain, not lower volatility. The resulting trade-off is asymmetric, with the relevance cost consistent across market phases while the gain is phase-dependent. The provider sets $m$ to read off exactly how much relevance each operating point costs.

title: Inferring Factor Importance with Explainable AI Model for Macrophage Immune Cell Polarization
abstract: Macrophages are highly plastic immune cells that dynamically shift between pro- and anti-inflammatory phenotypes in response to cytokines, transcriptional regulators, metabolic cues, and local microenvironment. Yet macrophage polarization is governed by nonlinear regulatory networks that are difficult to study experimentally. Here, we integrate mechanistic simulation, surrogate neural networks, and explainable machine learning to identify key regulatory drivers of polarization. We generated simulation data with a COPASI-based macrophage polarization model and used them to train an LSTM surrogate capable of reconstructing temporal macrophage marker dynamics across diverse macrophage activation states. SHAP, Individual Conditional Expectation, and Partial Dependence Plot analyses quantified feature importance, identified nonlinear response regimes, and characterized higher-order interactions among cytokines, transcription factors, and polarization markers. The model identified oxygen availability and IL10 as dominant anti-inflammatory regulators, consistently promoting M2-associated outputs such as ARG1 and VEGF. Conversely, IFN-γ, TNFα, IL12, iNOS, CXCL9, and mCXCL10 reinforced M1-associated inflammatory programs. STAT1-centered analyses identified iNOS, TNFα, and mCXCL10 levels as strong contributors to STAT1 outcomes, consistent with amplification of the IFN- γ/JAK/STAT1 inflammatory axis. VEGF negatively contributed to predicted STAT1 output, suggesting antagonism between M2 markers and M1 activation. SHAP, ICE, and PDP analyses also showed that STAT1 regulation is nonlinear and threshold-like: pro-inflammatory signals must accumulate before STAT1 rises sharply. Together, it demonstrates that the LSTM explainability framework can identify polarization drivers, uncover nonlinear regulatory thresholds, and prioritize pathways for experimental validation.
